blocks.text: But see more in the very learned book of the distinguished Scheffer, De militia navali. Not without reason, therefore, does the Philosopher compare to the two rudders of ships those twin legs of the locusts that we have mentioned, by which they in some way steer their motion. For when these are extended, they are lifted up either for a leap or for flight. Indeed, as is stated in the same place, ὅταν κάμψαντ᾽ ἐκτείνῃ πάλιν, ἀναγκαῖον ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἤρθαι [hotan kampsant' ekteinē palin, anankaion apo tēs gēs ērthai]: When they extend again what they have bent, they must be lifted from the ground. Accordingly Pisidas compares them to a bow, which is drawn back to shoot arrows. His words are:

Καὶ συλλέγει τὰ κῶλα, καὶ τείνει πάλιν, Ὥσπερ τὰ νεῦρα τῶν βελῶν οἱ τοξόται· Καὶ τραυματοῖ τὸ σῶμα τῶν ἐναντίων Τοῖς ἀντιλόξοις τῶν σκελῶν ἀκοντίοις. [Kai syllegei ta kōla, kai teinei palin, Hōsper ta neura tōn belōn hoi toxotai; Kai traumatoi to sōma tōn enantiōn Tois antiloxois tōn skelōn akontiois.]

And it draws in its limbs (that is, those hind legs) and stretches them out again, as archers do the strings of their arrows; and it wounds the body of its enemies with the slanting darts of its legs. What these verses mean entirely escaped the very learned translator, who first rendered the opening thus: Now it gathers corpses, now it scatters them. And in the last verse he wants to read τῶν βελῶν [tōn belōn] instead of τῶν σκελῶν [tōn skelōn].
